Lucy Lippard—a giant of American art criticism, author of more than 20 books, and co-founder of Printed Matter, the quintessential seller of books made by artists—turned 80 this year. Despite her multitude of other accomplishments, Lippard is best known for “The Dematerialization of Art,” an essay she co-authored in 1968 with John Chandler (available online here.) In the essay, Lippard presented evidence that art might be entering a phase of pure intellectualism, the result of which could be the complete disappearance of the traditional art object. The piece grew out of, and helped contextualize, the preceding decade or so of wildly inventive conceptual art, which often left behind only ephemeral, non-archival relics, or no relics at all other than perhaps recordings of experiences. Conceptual artists were devoted to making ideas the central focus of their work, and many argued convincingly that the objects artists make to express their ideas are nothing but waste products, and that the ideas themselves are the only things worthy of consideration. The essay was enormously influential at the time: so much so that Lippard followed it up with a book called Six Years, extensively analyzing evidence of the trend. But obviously in the long run her premonition was inaccurate since art objects still have yet to dematerialize. Nonetheless, in celebration of the upcoming 50th anniversary of the original publication of The Dematerialization of Art, we thought we would take a moment to delve into this influential essay and highlight what about it is relevant for our time.

Lippard based the core concepts she discussed in The Dematerialization of Art on an idea first laid out in a book called The Mathematical Basis of the Arts, written by the American painter Joseph Schillinger. In that book, Schillinger divided all of art history into five categories of aesthetic phenomena. First, he explained, came the “pre-aesthetic” phase of mimicry. Next came ritualistic or religious art. Then came emotional art. Then rational, empirical-based art. And then the fifth, and allegedly “final” aesthetic phase described by Schillinger was “scientific,” or what he called “post-aesthetic.” This final phase, he predicted, would culminate in the “liberation of the idea” and lead to the “disintegration of art.”

While contemplating the evolution of art throughout the 1950s and 60s, Lippard believed what she was witnessing was the emergence of this fifth phase of art. And she was excited about the notion. She considered dematerialization a positive, vital shift. After all, if the aesthetic object could cease to exist as the central focus of art then art could be freed from commodification, the often vile system that exerts so much destructive force on the lives and work of many artists.

As evidence that dematerialization had begun, Lippard cited movements such as Light and Space, which were visual but not object-based, and Minimalism, which drastically pared down the aesthetic object. Such movements she believed diminished the importance of the visual aspect of an artwork, defining the visual as more of a jumping-off point for an immaterial, intellectual experience. But one of the early, and obvious, criticisms of The Dematerialization of Art was that even though these ephemeral, conceptual concepts were less object-based, they still nonetheless resulted in physical phenomena. Even a performance artist creates a thing—a performance—which can be sold as an experience, or recorded.

No matter how slight a relic an artist creates, it can become fetishized and traded as a commodity. The only way to completely avoid the possibility of commodification is to never share an idea: then perhaps the reverence and sanctity of the intellectual experience can be preserved. But only shared ideas can truly be called art. And as soon as an idea is shared, it can be possessed, manipulated, and expressed in other ways, or other words, materialized. And as soon as something materializes it can be bought and sold as a commodity.

 Re-reading The Dematerialization of Art today, the only true error that seems evident is how it presents the five phases of art, as explained by Schillinger, as something linear. It is always tempting for each generation to see itself as standing at the forefront of modernity. Schillinger thought art had been progressing historically through phases, and Lippard thought she was part of the generation that was advancing art toward its evolutionary apex. But time does not move forward; it just passes. Culture is not linear; it repeats itself. Humanity devolves as rapidly as it evolves. And the truth was in the 1960s and 70s, and still is today, that artists are finding ways to dematerialize as rapidly as others are rediscovering how to materialize it.

Ultimately, Lippard must have also realized this even as she wrote on the topic of dematerialization because her essay concludes by asking if the so-called zero point in art is likely to be reached soon. The answer, she states, is, “It hardly seems likely.” Even today as artists sell virtual creations that exist only in digital space, we can still argue dematerialization is a fantasy. Anything that can be seen is by definition material, even if it can only be seen through virtual reality goggles. But in our opinion that only proves that perhaps achieving dematerialization was never really the point. The point Lippard was truly making was simply that one important aspect of visual art is to engage tirelessly in the search to discover how to express more with less. Any artist working toward dematerialization is also working toward simplicity. And simplicity leads to the discovery of what is truly indispensable, and thus truly meaningful. That is not the final phase of art. But it is capable of reminding us what the value of art truly is.

prompt: What are the side effects of taking too much medication for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder?
response_a:
Excessive use or misuse of medications prescribed for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) can lead to several side effects, including:

1. Insomnia: Stimulant medications used to treat ADHD can interfere with sleep patterns, leading to insomnia or difficulty falling asleep.

2. Decreased appetite and weight loss: Some stimulant medications may suppress appetite, resulting in weight loss.

3. Nausea and vomiting: Excessive intake of ADHD medications may cause nausea, vomiting, or stomach discomfort.

4. Increased heart rate and blood pressure: High doses of stimulants can increase heart rate and blood pressure, which can pose risks, particularly for individuals with pre-existing cardiac conditions.

5. Anxiety and irritability: Higher than recommended doses of ADHD medications may result in feelings of anxiety, restlessness, and irritability.

6. Depression: Prolonged use of ADHD medications at high doses has been associated with symptoms of depression.

7. Psychosis: In rare cases, excessive use of stimulant medications may cause psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, and paranoia.

It is essential to follow the prescribed dose and instructions provided by healthcare professionals to minimize the risk of adverse side effects from ADHD medications. Patients should also report any unwanted symptoms to their doctors immediately.
response_b:
While medication can be beneficial in managing symptoms of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), taking too much can lead to several unwanted side effects. Some common side effects of ADHD medications include:

1. Nausea and vomiting: This is one of the most commonly reported side effects, especially when starting treatment or increasing dosage.

2. Loss of appetite: Medications like stimulants can suppress appetite, leading to weight loss in some individuals.

3. Headaches: Headaches may occur as a result of changes in blood flow and pressure in the brain caused by the medication.

4. Insomnia: Stimulant medications can make it difficult to fall asleep or stay asleep, leading to sleep disturbances and daytime fatigue.

5. Dizziness: This can be caused by a drop in blood pressure, which may also result in fainting in some cases.

6. Dry mouth: Some medications used to treat ADHD can cause dryness in the mouth due to decreased saliva production.

7. Irritability and mood swings: High doses of stimulants can lead to mood changes such as irritability, agitation, and aggression.

8. Heart palpitations: Certain ADHD medications can increase heart rate and cause palpitations, particularly at higher doses.

9. Anxiety and restlessness: Higher doses of ADHD medications can cause feelings of anxiety and restlessness, particularly in children and adolescents.

It's important to follow your healthcare provider's instructions regarding medication dosage and to report any unusual symptoms or side effects immediately.

Akshara Slokam (അക്ഷര ശ്ലോകം) is a traditional way of Sloka chanting, a poetic entertainment developed in the Malayalam (മലയാളം) language of Kerala, India. It is in a classical format with strict rules on the meter of quatrains called slokas or mukthaka. A number of scholars sit to recite either Sanskrit or Malayalam slokas ( with more than eight letters in a line ). Once the recitation is started the next one in the turn has to recite a sloka having the first letter of the third line of the previous sloka. This resembles the north Indian Beit bazi.

It is mostly unused, but is active as the forerunner of the present day Anthakshari (അന്താക്ഷരി). Kairali Solaka Rangam Palai, Kundoor Smaraka Sadas and Amritabharathi Aksharashloka Samiti Chunangad are some of the famous Aksharasloka institutions in Kerala. Koonammoochi aksharaslokavedi and Ariyannur aksharaslokakalakshethram are worth mentioning for their contribution in the field of publishing many books related to aksharaslokam like aksharasloka directory (the first ever and the only one till date) containing names and addresses of aksharasloka artists. There are many active groups in Kerala from Kozhikode to Thiruvananthapuram with Trichur as the hub of the revival. There is a magazine dedicated for slokam called Kavana Kauthukam published from Trichur. Akhila Kerala Aksharasloka Parishath and Kerala Aksharasloka Federation are two organisations for propagating aksharaslokam. Competitions

Eventually it has been renamed now as "V. Kamalakara Menon Suvarna Mudra". The first winner of the Chakolas Gold Medal was late U.P. Raghava Warrier, popularly known as UPR. That was in 1955. “Weirs are either straightforward or they kill you” – Franco Ferrero: Author Whitewater Safety & Rescue
This statement is born out by the facts – 41 fatalities from only the five largest weir accidents in Europe! Almost all multiple fatalities in rafting, kayaking and canoeing are due to weirs.
Accidents involving Weirs in Europe:
2008 – 5 soldiers drown rafting on the Kander river in Switzerland
2008 – 13 people drown in a weir while canoeing on the Sava river in Slovenia
1999 – 4 UK tourists drown commercially rafting on the Salzach river in Austria
1993 – 9 German tourists die rafting on the Inn river in Engadine, Switzerland
1975 – 10 soldiers drown at Cromwell Weir on the river Trent in England
Weirs are so dangerous because even with correct swiftwater rescue training and equipment, if the weir has sufficient towback, it will be almost impossible to self rescue from. Looking at these accidents we can class them into different accident types:
1. Ignorance of the danger
The accidents that occurred on the Kander, Sava and Inn rivers where all, to a large extent, caused by a ignorance of the danger posed by the weirs. Most weirs look very tame compared to sections of whitewater, and the amount of aerated water bears no relation to the amount of towback that will be present. Changes in water level can also account for changes in the amount of towback at a weir. This was the case on the Inn, where the group had successfully run the weir the day before, when less water was flowing.
Ignorance can also mean not knowing that there is a weir (or other deadly feature) on the section of river that you are paddling. In 2010 a party of 4 Russian rafters died in Norway when they put in on the wrong section of the Sjoa river, one where the whole river flows through a siphon.
if there is any doubt that a weir (or rapid) is dangerous, then it should always be portaged.
2. Missing the take out
The other two accidents were caused by the rafts missing the take out. On the Trent this was during a military night exercise, on the Salzach when a guest fell out of the raft during landing. This can also be a problem when unrunnable gorges or hard rapids are downstream. Always have everyone look at the take out when there is such a deadly hazard downstream, and get out a good distance above it.
It is far better to walk an extra 200m than miss the last eddy! During night exercises lights positioned to show the end of the exercise area are needed to prevent people continuing downstream and into other hazards.
People often find it difficult to assess the danger posed by a man made weir, unless they are very experienced in understanding swiftwater. The Environmental agency in Great Britain needed to assess the danger that weirs on rivers posed to the public. Take a look at this comprehensive weir assessment system that Rescue 3 UK developed to help them with this difficult task.
The system is divided up into 4 sections:
1. Weir hazard rating
2. Likelihood of weir to cause harm rating
3. Weir risk rating (1 x 2)
4. Weir rescue rating
The Weir Hazard rating looks at 10 structural factors of the weir such as – the amount of towback, depth of hydraulic, height of the drop, etc. Each factor is then rated with points from 0 to 5, and all the points added up for a total score.

prompt: Explain the concept of social inclusion in 5 bullet points.
response_a:
1. Social inclusion refers to the active participation of individuals and groups in society, regardless of their backgrounds or circumstances. This includes access to resources, opportunities, and decision-making processes that enable them to fully contribute to their communities and benefit from societal advancements.

2. Social exclusion, on the other hand, describes the opposite - the marginalization and isolation of certain individuals or groups due to factors such as poverty, disability, ethnicity, or gender. This can result in a lack of access to education, employment, healthcare, and other basic needs, perpetuating cycles of disadvantage and deprivation.

3. Promoting social inclusion requires efforts at multiple levels, including individual, organizational, and systemic change. At the individual level, this may involve building self-confidence, developing skills, and fostering positive relationships. Organizations can promote social inclusion by ensuring equal access to services and resources, valuing diverse perspectives, and providing opportunities for leadership and advancement. Systemic changes may include policies that address structural inequality, such as affirmative action or income redistribution.

4. The benefits of social inclusion are numerous and far-reaching. For individuals, it can lead to improved health, increased self-esteem, and enhanced social networks. Communities can benefit from increased economic activity, reduced crime rates, and greater cohesion and resilience. Society as a whole can enjoy higher levels of social capital, greater innovation, and a more equitable distribution of resources.

5. However, promoting social inclusion also presents challenges and obstacles, particularly in societies that have historically perpetuated exclusionary practices. Addressing these barriers may require addressing systemic prejudices, overcoming institutionalized inequalities, and challenging deeply ingrained cultural norms. Nevertheless, the potential rewards of social inclusion make it a worthwhile goal, both for individual wellbeing and collective prosperity.
response_b:
1. Social inclusion refers to the process of ensuring that all individuals and groups, regardless of their backgrounds or characteristics, have equal opportunities to participate fully in society. This can be achieved through policies and practices that promote equality, accessibility, and integration.

2. Social inclusion involves addressing systemic barriers that prevent certain populations from participating fully in society, such as poverty, lack of education, disability, ethnicity, and gender. It requires recognizing and respecting the unique needs and perspectives of these groups and taking steps to address their specific challenges.

3. Social inclusion also involves promoting social cohesion and reducing social exclusion. This means fostering a sense of community and belonging among diverse groups, and working to reduce prejudice, discrimination, and isolation. It requires creating environments that are welcoming, inclusive, and supportive of all individuals.

4. Social inclusion is not just about providing services and resources; it's also about empowering individuals and communities to take an active role in shaping their own lives and futures. This involves providing opportunities for participation, leadership, and decision-making, as well as supporting self-determination and autonomy.

5. Finally, social inclusion is a continuous process that requires ongoing monitoring, evaluation, and improvement. It requires a commitment to learning, innovation, and collaboration, as well as a willingness to adapt and respond to changing circumstances and emerging needs. It requires a shared responsibility among all members of society to work together to create a more inclusive and equitable future.

Introduction
The recent development of compact light sources in the terahertz band has led to the frontier research field of terahertz wave spectroscopy. Several vibration modes exist in the terahertz region characteristic of molecules, and measurement of terahertz wave spectra is widely used to identify materials. A major advantage of a terahertz light source using an accelerator is its high peak power, leading to the development of various light sources such as free-electron lasers (FELs) and coherent radiation. With the development of accelerator technology, various techniques have been developed to produce short-pulse electron bunches. Consequently, active research and development of terahertz light sources using accelerators have been conducted. In particular, at Nihon University, various types of terahertz light sources have been developed over the past decade. At the straight sections of FELs, coherent synchrotron radiation (CSR) and coherent edge radiation (CER) have been developed and implemented, and the produced light has been transmitted to laboratories through FEL beamlines. As these terahertz light sources can be used simultaneously with infrared FELs, they are used for experiments including those involving biologic tissue imaging. Further, at the straight sections of parametric X-ray radiation (PXR), coherent transition radiation (CTR) with a power output of one millijoule per macro-pulse has been developed and implemented, which can be used in laboratories via PXR beamlines. Additionally, prospective application of CTR in product management of tablets is being researched.
A terahertz light source produced in an accelerator also serves as an excellent tool for evaluation of the accelerator. In advanced accelerators like X-ray FELs, the size of an electron bunch is comparable to that of the wavelength of terahertz light. Therefore, it is possible to measure the shape of a bunch by measuring the spectrum of coherent radiation produced by that electron bunch. To date, streak cameras and RF deflectors are the only tools that have been developed to measure bunch shapes. However, the time resolution of conventional streak cameras is insufficient to measure sub-ps bunch lengths. Further, electron bunches are often distorted by conventional RF deflectors, making it impossible to non-destructively measure the states of electron bunches prior to FEL oscillation. Additionally, in the case of electron beams with high repetition frequency, such as X-ray FELs using superconducting linear accelerators that are currently under development, it is difficult to measure the bunch length for each micro-pulse via the existing methods.
Given these circumstances, we conducted measurements of bunch length using CSR that was capable of non-destructively observing electron beams. As the light source, we utilized the CSR source in the terahertz band that had been developed at the LEBRA accelerator facility at Nihon University. Such bunch length measurements obtained using coherent radiation produced by electron bunches have also been studied and used in several accelerator facilities. However, unlike other studies, we succeeded in measuring the root-mean-square (RMS) bunch length with high precision by strictly considering the detector’s characteristic sensitivity during the observation of the coherent radiation. In the present study, we first outline the CSR light source from Nihon University that was used. Following this, we discuss the proposed measurement technology that is capable of detecting small changes in bunch length using the narrow-band characteristic of the detector. On the basis of the results obtained, we conclude that a correlation exists between electron bunch charge and bunch length for high-charge bunches.
2. Coherent Synchrotron Radiation Source at LEBRA
The LEBRA Linac at Nihon University consists of a DC electron gun of 100 kV, one buncher, three S-Band 4 m acceleration tubes and two high-frequency source klystrons, as depicted in Figure 1. Its operating acceleration frequency is 2856 MHz, the acceleration energy is 40–100 MeV, the repetition rate is 2–10 Hz and the macro-pulse width of the associated beam is 5–20 μs. Besides the normal full-bunch mode operation, the electron gun system is capable of operating in a high-charge burst mode at intervals of 1/64 or 1/128 using a high-speed grid pulser of 600 ps full width at half maximum (FWHM). How to bypass a paywall (easy guide)
Reading time: 6 min
Imagine you are in your flow doing research, browsing through articles, and trying to make sense of the volumes of info you’ve been rapidly uploading into your brain. And BAAM! 💥

If you are not a regular reader, you will probably close the tab and find another article. Or ditch the idea entirely.

What is a paywall
A paywall is a way to restrict access to a website (most commonly publications) by soliciting a purchase or a subscription.

Soft paywalls allow users to access some content by limiting you to several articles per month. Example: Medium.com.

Hard paywalls will restrict content to be accessible only to the subscribed users. Example: Trends.co.

There are two categories of paywalls: client-side and server-side paywalls. The difference between client and server-side paywalls is the order in which your browser will load content.

Client-side paywall will first load the content into your browser and then check if the user has the appropriate permissions to view the content. If the user doesn’t have access, the website will create an overlay element to hide the loaded content. Since the content has been loaded already, you can access it with extensions that extract the HTML from the website.

In the case of server-side paywalls, the only option we have is to try to trick websites into thinking that we are a search engine bot, which are most commonly authorized to view content.

Bypass Paywalls with Chrome Extensions 
The easiest way to bypass a paywall is to use reading extensions such as Reader Mode. 

Reader Mode will take the body of an article and convert it into a pretty and distraction-free format. Most importantly, it will remove the overlay elements that made it impossible to read the restricted article.

You can set a keyboard shortcut to bypass a paywall in seconds. You can customize the shortcut by navigating to chrome://extensions/shortcuts.

Alternatively, you can also bypass a paywall with the Pocket. Pocket is a Chrome extension that saves articles to be read in the future and formats them nicely. To bypass a paywall with Pocket:

Save To Pocket → Open My List → Click on the article

Bardeen is a no-code productivity app that allows you to run automations right from the browser.

After you install the extension and create a free account, you can access content hidden behind a paywall by running one of the following pre-built playbooks. 

Remove a hard paywall with web archives

Organic traffic is the bread and butter of digital media companies. And thus, they optimize their platforms for search engines. 

This means that media websites treat web crawlers and regular visitors differently. 

A regular user will land on a page with a hard paywall, whereas crawlers will get full access to the article so that it can be indexed.

The duration of an IV infusion can vary depending on the substance being administered and the rate at which it's delivered, typically ranging from several minutes to a few hours. prompt: What is the difference between corporatism and socialism, and can a capitalist economy be considered corporatist or socialist?
response_a:
Corporatism and socialism are two distinct economic systems with significant differences. While both aim to address societal issues, they have contrasting approaches to achieving their goals.

Socialism is an economic system that advocates for collective ownership and control of resources, production, and distribution. Socialist societies prioritize the needs of society over individual interests, and wealth and resources are distributed based on need rather than merit. The state plays a central role in managing the economy, and the goal is to eliminate social inequality and promote equality for all.

On the other hand, corporatism is an economic system characterized by close collaboration between the government, businesses, and labor unions. Corporatism aims to balance the interests of these stakeholders and promote social harmony while maintaining a capitalist economy. In this system, businesses are encouraged to collaborate with the government to develop policies that benefit all parties involved, including employees, consumers, and shareholders. The state's role in managing the economy is more limited than in socialism, and market forces still play a crucial role in driving economic growth.

It is essential to note that while corporatism is compatible with a capitalist economy, it does not necessarily imply that every capitalist economy is corporatist. While some capitalist economies may exhibit elements of corporatism, such as Germany, Austria, and Switzerland, others like the United States do not adhere to this model. The U.S. Economic system is predominantly capitalist, with private enterprise and market competition driving economic activity, with minimal state intervention beyond regulatory functions.

In summary, while corporatism and socialism share some similarities, their fundamental principles differ significantly. Socialism prioritizes collective ownership and control of resources and distribution of wealth based on need, whereas corporatism seeks to balance the interests of businesses, labor unions, and the state through collaboration. A capitalist economy can be corporatist but is not inherently so.
response_b:
Corporatism and socialism are two distinct economic systems with fundamental differences. While both systems aim to address societal needs and inequalities, they differ in their approaches to achieving these goals.

Socialism is an economic system characterized by public ownership and control of key industries and resources. The primary goal of socialism is to redistribute wealth more evenly across society, eliminate poverty, and provide for the common good. Socialist economies typically have a strong emphasis on collective decision-making and community welfare, rather than individual profit-seeking.

On the other hand, corporatism is a form of economic organization that emphasizes cooperation and collaboration between business, labor, and government. Corporatism seeks to balance the interests of various stakeholders within an economy, including employers, workers, consumers, and the state. It aims to promote social justice, economic stability, and national development through coordinated action among these groups.

While corporatism shares some similarities with socialism, such as a focus on social welfare and economic planning, it differs significantly in its approach to resource allocation and ownership. In a corporatist economy, private ownership and market competition are still prominent features, while in socialism, ownership and decision-making are primarily held by the state.

It's possible for a capitalist economy to incorporate elements of corporatism, as many modern economies have moved towards greater regulation, social welfare programs, and collaboration between business, labor, and government. However, a purely corporatist economy would require a significant departure from traditional capitalist principles, as it would entail greater state intervention in the economy and a redistribution of power away from private actors. Therefore, while corporatism may coexist with capitalism in practice, it is not a synonym for socialism, which fundamentally challenges the private ownership and profit motive at the heart of capitalist economics.

prompt: How can I write a compelling story about an investigation? Include key details and elements to include, and how to keep the reader engaged.
response_a:
Writing a compelling story about an investigation requires a delicate balance between solving the mystery and keeping the reader engaged. Here are some key details and elements you should consider:

1. Establish the crime or mystery: Introduce the crime or mystery that needs to be solved. Make sure it's intriguing and raises questions in the reader's mind. Provide enough information to hook the reader but not so much that they figure out the solution right away.

2. Introduce your protagonist: The investigator is the heart of your story. Make them relatable, flawed, and determined. Give them a backstory that explains their motivations for pursuing this case.

3. Create suspense: Use pacing and tension to build suspense. Alternate moments of action with moments of reflection, and use cliffhangers to keep the reader on the edge of their seat.

4. Develop your suspects: Create a cast of characters with plausible motives and alibis. Drop subtle hints that might suggest one person's guilt over another.

5. Incorporate red herrings: Don't make it too easy for the reader to guess the culprit. Inject false leads and misdirections to throw off the trail.

6. Show the investigation process: Describe the methods and techniques used by your detective to uncover evidence. Make the process seem logical and believable.

7. Keep the stakes high: Raise the stakes as the story progresses. Make the consequences of failure more severe. This will create a sense of urgency and keep the reader invested.

8. Resolve the mystery: When all is said and done, provide a satisfying resolution. Tie up loose ends and reveal the truth behind the crime.

9. End on a strong note: Close the story with a powerful final scene that leaves the reader feeling satisfied.

To keep the reader engaged throughout the story, use vivid descriptions, dialogue, and sensory details to bring the scenes to life. Avoid info-dumping and exposition dumps; instead, weave information into the narrative naturally. Finally, ensure your story has a clear structure with a beginning, middle, and end. By following these guidelines, you can create a gripping investigation story that will leave your readers on the edge of their seats.
response_b:
Writing a compelling story about an investigation requires a balance between providing enough details to create suspense and mystery while also moving the plot forward. Here are some key details and elements to consider:

1. Introduce the investigator: Begin by introducing your main character, whether it's a seasoned detective or an amateur sleuth. Provide some background information that will help the reader understand their motivations and skills.

2. Establish the crime: Clearly define the nature of the crime being investigated. Is it a murder, theft, or something else entirely? Be sure to provide enough information for the reader to have a clear understanding of what has happened.

3. Build tension: Keep the reader guessing by withholding key details and dropping subtle clues throughout the story. Use descriptive language to create a sense of foreboding and unease.

4. Develop suspects: As the investigation progresses, introduce potential suspects with distinct personalities and motives. Make the reader question who might be responsible for the crime.

5. Incorporate red herrings: Don't make it too easy for the reader to solve the case. Inject false leads and misdirection to keep them guessing until the very end.

6. Explore the investigative process: Show the investigator's methods and techniques as they gather evidence and interview witnesses. This will add realism and depth to the story.

7. Create a satisfying resolution: When the case is finally solved, make sure the ending is both surprising and satisfying. Tie up loose ends and provide closure for the characters involved.

To keep the reader engaged, consider using short chapters, cliffhangers, and dialogue-heavy scenes. Use vivid descriptions to bring the setting and characters to life, and incorporate twists and turns that will keep the reader on the edge of their seat. Lastly, avoid excessive exposition or overly complex plotlines, as these can lose the reader's interest. Stick to a simple, well-paced narrative that keeps the focus on the investigation at hand.

The Royal Gibraltar Post Office is the postal services in the British overseas territory of Gibraltar. It is currently a department within the Government of Gibraltar.

History

The Gibraltar Post Office has been running for over 150 years, as in 1857 the Overland Post Office (based in the colonial authorities' premises at Secretary's Lane) merged with the Packet Agency (which had office's in Turnbull's Lane). The first stamps went on sale in September and a year later a new building was completed and opened at 104 Main Street. This remains the main post office in Gibraltar today.

In 1886 the local colonial authorities took over control of the Gibraltar Post Office and were able to issue their own stamps. Initially they overprinted Bermuda stamps but by December they had their own design. However, they still sold Spanish stamps if required and between 1889 and 1898 the post office sold Gibraltar stamps valued in pesetas as this was the currency in circulation.

For the first fifty years, the Gibraltar Post Office had responsibility for the post office not only in Gibraltar but also for the British postal service in Morocco. This ended in 1907.

In 2005 the Gibraltar Post Office was granted the title of "Royal" by Her Majesty the Queen. Gibraltar is the only Commonwealth or British Overseas Territory post office outside the United Kingdom that bears this title. Gibraltar has traditional red pillar boxes and the tops are also frequently painted black.

The Post Office continues to provide some traditional services and was still using benefit books after they were abandoned in the United Kingdom, while there is also a special philatelic counter to sell the commemorative stamps.

The Post office provides a next day delivery service to the community with letters posted before 07.00 that day in any of the 30+ pillar boxes located in Gibraltar delivered same day. As the official designated postal operator by the UPU (Universal Postal Union) it has a universal service obligation to deliver mail to every Gibraltar resident and provide an international mail service to all UPU member countries worldwide (192 member countries)

Services
The Royal Gibraltar Post Office provides the following services:
Letter post
Parcel post
Airmail
Express mail services
Poste restante
Post office boxes
Registration services
Postal orders

Banking facilities are provided through the Gibraltar Savings Bank, which is part of the Gibraltar Government services.

Office locations

The Royal Gibraltar Post Office has a number of offices around Gibraltar:
Main Office - A Victorian building which sits in Main Street.
P.O. Boxes Unit - Irish Town
Mail Operations Centre and Parcel Post - Unit E, Admiral Rooke Road

The North District Post Office in Glacis Road and the South District Post Office in Scud Hill were closed in late 2014 for refurbishment, but in February 2016 had still not reopened. In September of that year, the Government stated that there were no plans to reopen either Post Office; Minister Joe Bossano explained there had been a proposal to house Savings Bank outlets in the premises but that when the money generated was considered, it was found not to be financially viable.

The Cedar Tavern (or Cedar Street Tavern) was a bar and restaurant at the eastern edge of Greenwich Village, New York City. In its heyday, known as a gathering place for avant garde writers and artists, it was located at 24 University Place, near 8th Street. It was famous in its day as a hangout of many prominent Abstract Expressionist painters and Beat writers and poets. It closed in April 1963 and reopened three blocks north in 1964, at 82 University Place, between 11th and 12th Streets.

History

1860s-1950s 
The Cedar Tavern was opened in 1866 on Cedar Street, near present day Zuccotti Park. In 1933 it moved north to 55 West Eighth Street. In 1945 it moved east to 24 University Place. In 1955, the Cedar Tavern was purchased by Sam Diliberto, a butcher, and his brother in law, John Bodnar, a window washer, from Joe Provenzano.

1950s 
Robert Motherwell had a studio nearby in the early 1950s, and he held a weekly salon for artists there. The Cedar was the closest place for them to have a drink afterwards.  Habitués liked it for its cheap drinks and lack of tourists or middle-class squares. University Place in those days was downmarket because of the several welfare and single-room occupancy hotels in the area. Jackson Pollock, Willem de Kooning, Mark Rothko, Franz Kline, Michael Goldberg, Landes Lewitin, Aristodimos Kaldis, Phillip Guston, Knute Stiles, Ted Joans, James Brooks, Charles Cajori, Mercedes Matter, Howard Kanovitz, Al Leslie, Stanley Twardowicz, Morton Feldman, John Cage, and others of the New York School all patronized the bar in the 1950s when many lived in or near Greenwich Village. After a year they bought the building at 82 University Place, which had been occupied by an antique store, and built the new bar in a more upscale pub style. This proved prescient; in the wake of Joe Diliberto's death on October 27, 2007, his brother Mike failed to reopen the establishment.

When the Cedar Tavern closed in 2006, its century-old, 50 foot mahogany bar was sold to Austin businessmen, John M. Scott and Eddy Patterson. In 2016, it was brought out of storage to serve as the centerpiece of Eberly, a restaurant in Austin, Texas.

I would guess even the most brilliant, experienced, educated-about-teens parent has felt the same sentiments as you about their teenager's behavior: "I don't know why or what to do." Although research suggests that a majority of adolescents are not the reckless, rude nightmares of stereotypes, most still have their mystifying moments.

The reasons for your daughter's attitude might be complex and personal to her, and impossible to understand without meeting and talking to her. However, some simple explanations that could apply to many teens at this age might be helpful to consider.

There's a lot going on for teenagers. Their emotions can feel like a rollercoaster, and they're clambering toward independence. Since you are their safe person, they may feel safest lashing out at you.

Your emotions live in your brain's limbic system, where they light up when you feel them—pleasant or unpleasant. Studies have shown that for adolescents, this limbic system affected by puberty hormonal changes results in increased emotional outbursts and impulsivity.  Imagine your annoyance when someone asks you to do something you don't want to do and triple it in your teen's brain.

Adults have the impulse control to manage or lower intensity annoyance by holding back so they can respond respectfully. This can take double the effort for teenagers, whose brains are still developing and maturing. Picture your teen's brain lighting up with fireworks of frustration as they react in a way that appears to be completely out of proportion to the source. This image might at least help you keep your cool when your teen can't.

Another formative part of adolescent development is testing limits. It's not a conscious, "What happens if I let my emotions fly when my mom asks me to clean up?" but rather a learned association: When I flip out because I don't want to help around the house, mom backs off and I don't have to do it.

The limits can be emotional as well: Your teen may not know where or how else to unleash all this intense emotion, so they fling it at you. If nothing too terrible happens, this can become a pattern that feels easier to them than the hard work of regulating these intense emotions on their own.

It is well known that children behave differently with their parents. Sometimes that means they save their worst tantrums for when you are alone with them or fall apart at home after a day of holding it together at school. That's because they know (hopefully) you love them no matter how they act.

In the bestselling book about raising teenage girls, Untangled, Lisa Damour, Ph.D. presents the upside of an argumentative teen: They feel safe speaking up and fighting for their perspective. Dr. Damour suggests that highly obedient teens can be more likely to rebel in a secretive way that can pose more risk.

If your teen openly debates and argues with you, it means they trust they can do so without losing your love and support. So, ironically, if you have a teen "with attitude," it might be a sign they are developing their independence within a trusting relationship with you.

All of these understandable reasons for teenagers acting out don't give them full reign to behave and treat you however they want just because you love them unconditionally. You can have empathy for their emotions while placing boundaries around their behaviors.

Teens are often compared to toddlers in terms of the primal nature of their emotions. Although adolescents obviously have a lot more skills than toddlers, their emotions can feel just as out of control. As their brains change, along with the demands of their environments from the social to the academic, they need to develop more sophisticated self-regulation strategies than what worked at younger ages.

Connect with your teen during a calm, peaceful moment to identify the problem ("lashing out"), its natural consequences (high stress and conflict between you), and possible replacements for lashing out (emotion regulation strategies). It helps to name what would motivate them to change, such as less arguing.

It might help to make a visual list of emotional regulation strategies to help get into the habit of using them. 
Common strategies include:

-Going for a walk or run.
-Listening to music.
-Writing in a journal.
-Drawing.
-Connecting with a friend.

If teens can learn ways to calm themselves in the moment, they can better do the next critical step: Discuss their stress and emotions directly with you rather than taking them out on you.

Within all of this support for their emotions, maintain your behavioral expectations. Helping around the house and responding to you respectfully even if in disagreement should still be expected.

There can be a wide range of teenage behavior that fits on the continuum of "normal," no matter how aggravating. However, you may want to get your teen a psychological evaluation if you notice the following:

-Irritability dominates your teen's mood.
-They seem to have difficulty enjoying activities.
-You notice other significant changes in sleep, appetite, or behaviors.

A mental health professional with expertise in adolescents can do an assessment to ensure a mental health condition like depression or anxiety is not underlying what you are observing. If your teen is experiencing symptoms at the level of a mental health diagnosis, the sooner they get help, the better.

prompt: What are some of the most important factors that influence investor decisions?
response_a:

Investors analyze various financial metrics such as earnings per share (EPS), revenue growth, profit margins, and return on investment (ROI) to determine the potential returns they can expect from investing in a particular stock.

2. Market Trends: The overall market trends also play a significant role in influencing investor decisions. Investors closely monitor economic indicators such as interest rates, inflation, and GDP to predict how the economy will perform in the future and adjust their portfolios accordingly.

3. Company Management: The quality and experience of a company's management team are essential considerations for investors. They evaluate the track record of the CEO, CFO, and other executives to assess their ability to lead the company and make sound business decisions.

4. Competitive Landscape: The competitive landscape of an industry can significantly impact investor decisions. Investors analyze the strengths and weaknesses of a company's competitors to determine its position in the market and whether it has a sustainable competitive advantage.

5. Industry Trends: Investors also pay close attention to industry trends and disruptive technologies that could impact a company's performance. They evaluate whether a company is well-positioned to capitalize on emerging opportunities or whether it faces significant threats from new entrants or technological disruptions.

6. Valuation: Investors use various valuation methods such as price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, price-to-book (P/B) ratio, and discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis to determine a company's intrinsic value and compare it to its current stock price. This helps them decide whether a stock is overvalued, undervalued, or fairly priced.

7. Risk Appetite: Every investor has a different risk appetite, which influences their investment decisions. Some investors prefer high-risk, high-reward stocks, while others opt for more conservative investments with lower risks. Understanding an investor's risk tolerance is crucial when making recommendations.

8. Regulatory Environment: The regulatory environment in which a company operates can have a significant impact on its performance and investor decisions. Investors monitor regulatory changes, legal challenges, and compliance issues to assess the potential risks and opportunities associated with a company.

prompt: What are some tips for running in the winter months? Consider factors such as clothing, diet, and overall training plan.
response_a:
1. Dress appropriately: In colder weather, it's essential to wear layers that will keep you warm but also allow for moisture wicking and breathability. Start with a base layer made of synthetic or wool material to wick away sweat, then add an insulating middle layer, and finish with a waterproof and windproof outer layer. Don't forget to cover your extremities too, wearing a hat, gloves, and thick socks.

2. Adjust your training schedule: Shorter days and poorer weather conditions may make it challenging to stick to your regular training routine. Consider adjusting your schedule to run during daylight hours or invest in a good headlamp if you prefer running early in the morning or late at night. You could also switch up your route to take advantage of well-lit areas or indoor tracks when the weather is particularly bad.

3. Fuel your body properly: The winter months can be demanding on our bodies, especially when trying to maintain a consistent training regime. Make sure you fuel your body properly by eating foods rich in carbohydrates, protein, and healthy fats. These nutrients will provide you with the energy you need to power through your runs while keeping you warm. Avoid consuming large meals before going out for a run as this can lead to discomfort and cramps.

4. Stay hydrated: Although we tend to drink less water in colder temperatures due to reduced sweating, it's still essential to stay hydrated during winter runs. Dehydration can negatively impact performance and increase the risk of injury. Aim to drink around 17-20 ounces of water two to three hours before your run and carry a water bottle or hydration pack to ensure you have access to fluids throughout your run.

5. Mix up your workouts: Running in snow, ice, or slush can be dangerous and challenging. Consider incorporating cross-training activities into your routine, such as strength training, yoga, or cycling, to help build overall fitness and prevent injuries. By varying your workouts, you can challenge yourself in new ways and prevent boredom.

6. Listen to your body: Winter weather can put additional stress on your joints and muscles, leading to increased soreness and injury risks. If you experience any pain or discomfort during your runs, it's essential to listen to your body and rest when needed.
response_b:
1. Dress appropriately: In colder weather, it's essential to layer your clothing to keep warm without overheating. Start with a base layer made of moisture-wicking material, followed by an insulating layer, and finish with a windproof and waterproof outer layer. Don't forget to cover your head, hands, and feet as they are more susceptible to cold.

2. Fuel up: Winter running can burn more calories due to the added effort required to move through snow or ice. Make sure to eat a balanced diet rich in carbohydrates, proteins, and healthy fats to provide the energy you need for your runs. Stay hydrated as well, even if it's not as hot outside.

3. Adjust your training plan: The shorter days and harsher conditions may impact your training schedule. Try to run during daylight hours when possible, and consider adding indoor workouts or cross-training activities like strength training or cycling to your routine. Also, be aware that your pace may slow down due to the extra effort required in slippery or snowy conditions.

4. Be visible: With less daylight in the winter, it's crucial to wear reflective clothing and use lights or a headlamp to make yourself visible to other runners, cars, and pedestrians. This will help ensure your safety while running.

5. Listen to your body: Winter running can put additional strain on your joints and muscles due to the hard surfaces and icy conditions. Be mindful of any pain or discomfort and adjust your training plan accordingly. Rest and recovery are just as important as the actual running, so don't push yourself too hard.

6. Warm up properly: Before heading out into the cold, make sure to warm up inside for a few minutes to get your blood flowing and prevent injury. This could include dynamic stretches, jumping jacks, or high knees.

7. Keep moving: If you find yourself stuck in icy or snowy conditions, try to maintain forward motion instead of stopping suddenly. This will help prevent falls and slips.

Remember, winter running requires preparation and caution, but it can also be a rewarding experience. By following these tips, you can stay safe, warm, and motivated throughout the season.

prompt: What is the difference between a station wagon and a SUV?
response_a:
While both station wagons and SUVs (Sports Utility Vehicles) serve as passenger vehicles, there are some key differences between the two:

1. Body Style: The most apparent difference between the two is their body style. Station wagons have a traditional sedan-like body with a sleek design and a sloping roofline that gradually tapers towards the rear. In contrast, SUVs have a boxy shape with a raised ride height, providing better ground clearance for off-road driving.

2. Passenger Capacity: Station wagons generally offer seating for up to five passengers, while larger models can accommodate seven people. SUVs, on the other hand, provide more spacious interiors with ample room for up to seven or eight passengers, depending on the model.

3. Cargo Space: Station wagons typically offer less cargo space than SUVs due to their sloping rooflines. However, they make up for it by offering a flatter load floor, making it easier to load and unload items. SUVs provide a higher cargo area, but due to their steeply raked rear windows, loading and unloading can be more challenging.

4. Off-Road Capability: SUVs are designed for off-road driving and feature four-wheel drive systems, skid plates, and high ground clearance. They also offer features like hill descent control and low-range gearing. Station wagons are not built for off-roading and typically come with front-wheel drive or all-wheel drive configurations.

5. Performance: Due to their lower center of gravity and lighter bodyweight, station wagons tend to handle better on paved roads than SUVs. SUVs, however, offer better towing capacity and can handle rough terrain more effectively.

In summary, while both station wagons and SUVs serve as practical family vehicles, their differences in body style, passenger and cargo capacity, off-road capability, and performance cater to different needs and preferences.
response_b:
While both station wagons and SUVs (Sports Utility Vehicles) serve as passenger vehicles with cargo space, there are some key differences between the two:

1. Body Style: The primary difference between a station wagon and an SUV is their body style. A station wagon is essentially an extended version of a sedan with a trunk that can be accessed by swinging doors at the back. In contrast, an SUV has a boxy design with a raised ground clearance and a separate cargo area that is typically accessed through a tailgate.

2. Purpose: Station wagons were traditionally designed for families who needed extra cargo space for camping trips or transporting sports equipment. They offer a comfortable ride, better fuel efficiency, and easier handling due to their lower center of gravity. SUVs, on the other hand, were originally created for off-road adventures, providing higher ground clearance, four-wheel drive, and more rugged features such as tow hooks and skid plates. Nowadays, many people opt for SUVs as family cars due to their spacious interiors, versatility, and perceived safety benefits.

3. Size: Station wagons tend to be smaller than SUVs and are often classified as midsize sedans with extended rear ends. This makes them more practical for urban environments where parking spaces are tight. SUVs, on the other hand, come in various sizes, from compact to full-size models, making them suitable for different purposes and needs.

4. Price: Generally, station wagons are less expensive than SUVs due to their simpler designs and lighter materials used in construction. However, this can vary depending on the specific model and features selected.

5. Resale Value: Station wagons have historically had lower resale values compared to SUVs because they are less popular and demand for them is lower. SUVs, especially larger models, tend to hold onto their value better over time due to their popularity and utility.

In summary, while both station wagons and SUVs serve similar functions, their differences in body style, purpose, size, price, and resale value make them distinct options for buyers looking for a vehicle that meets their specific needs.

One 2017 article notes that beef liver may sometimes contain detectable levels of antibiotics, which could be hazardous to human health. This could be due to animals receiving antibiotics close to the time of their slaughter.

Antibiotic residues present in food may result in antibiotic resistance and cause:

allergic reactions
anaphylaxis
toxicity
disruptions in embryo development
certain types of cancer

Concerns about beef liver
Many people may avoid eating beef liver due to health concerns, including cholesterol, toxicity, and an overload of iron.

However, the potential health benefits of consuming beef liver typically outweigh these concerns.

Cholesterol
Due to the liver naturally producing cholesterol, beef liver contains roughly 274 mgTrusted Source of cholesterol per 100 g, making it a high cholesterol food. Due to this, many people may wish to avoid eating it.

Certain people may wish to consider avoiding or minimizing their consumption of beef liver, as it may interact with other health factors or issues they have.

Include key characteristics, examples, and an explanation of their similarities and differences. Provide a conclusion that summarizes the main points and emphasizes the significance of understanding clusters and groups in organizations and society.
response_a:
A cluster refers to a collection of closely related entities or objects that are located in proximity to each other due to shared attributes, needs, or functions. Clusters can be physical or virtual, and they often form naturally as a result of market forces, technological advancements, or geographical constraints. The key characteristics of a cluster include spatial concentration, specialization, interdependence, and knowledge spillovers.

One example of a cluster is Silicon Valley in California, which is home to many high-tech companies, research institutions, and venture capital firms. These entities are concentrated in a specific geographic area due to factors such as access to talent, infrastructure, and funding. They also share a common focus on innovation, entrepreneurship, and cutting-edge technologies, which has led to the emergence of new products, services, and industries. Another example is the fashion district in New York City, where designers, manufacturers, and retailers work together to create and distribute clothing and accessories.

In contrast, a group refers to a collection of individuals who share a common identity, purpose, or affiliation, but may not necessarily have close spatial proximity or functional interdependence. Groups can be formal or informal, temporary or permanent, and based on various criteria such as age, gender, ethnicity, religion, profession, or interest. The key characteristics of a group include social cohesion, communication, decision-making, and leadership.

For example, a sports team is a type of group that consists of athletes with diverse backgrounds and skills who come together to compete against other teams. They may practice and play games in different locations, but they share a common goal, strategy, and culture. Another example is a professional association, which brings together people with similar occupational or academic qualifications to exchange knowledge, resources, and opportunities.

The similarities between clusters and groups are that they both involve aggregations of entities or individuals with some degree of interaction and interdependence. However, the differences lie in the nature and intensity of these relationships. Clusters tend to be more focused on economic or functional outcomes, while groups tend to be more concerned with social or psychological outcomes. Clusters are also more static and bounded, while groups are more dynamic and open to external influences.

Understanding clusters and groups is significant for organizations and society because they provide insights into how networks and communities emerge, evolve, and contribute to economic growth, social cohesion, and environmental sustainability

The coronavirus and resulting increase in government regulation will continue to cause detrimental economic impact to businesses and individuals. This adverse impact on revenues and expenses will create challenges in meeting obligations under contracts. A properly drafted force majeure clause can help, but what happens if the force majeure clause is too narrow or the contract simply does not include one? Companies should know they may still have a legal basis under Oklahoma law to avoid or limit contractual obligations that have become impossible or impracticable to perform.

Impossibility and impracticability are closely related, but technically distinguishable, doctrines. Impossibility is a common law defense while impracticability is a Uniform Commercial Code defense. Oklahoma courts generally do not distinguish between impossibility and impracticability because the terms are of equal legal effect. In either case, a party's performance is excused if it has become "impossible" or "totally unreasonable or impracticable" due to an event outside of the party's control and that the party could not reasonably foresee when executing the contract.

A duty is impossible to perform if it cannot be accomplished by any means. Impracticability requires extreme and unreasonable difficulty, expense, injury, or loss. As a result, changes in market forces do not render performance impracticable unless far outside the normal range, because they are the sort of risk that commercial contracts are intended to cover. Whereas severe shortages due to exigencies such as war, embargo, local crop failure, or unforeseen shutdown of major sources of supply that cause a marked increase in cost or prevent performance may render performance impracticable. Even when performance is impossible or impracticable, parties must use reasonable efforts to surmount any obstacles to performance and must continue to perform those portions of obligations that are possible or practicable.

For example, courts in Oklahoma have held that it was impossible or impracticable: for an employer to comply with the terms of a settlement agreement requiring it to use the plaintiff as a back-up machine operator, where the company stopped using the machine and there was no need for an operator or backup operator; for a lessor to restore a tornado-demolished hotel, where the hotel could not be reasonably reconstructed or the defendant could not obtain the necessary materials due to a state of war; and for a railroad to continue shipping grain, where the railroad ceased operations following the construction of a dam that flooded 19 miles of tracks and which would have cost $25 million in today's dollars to relocate.

In contrast, an Oklahoma court has held that it was not impossible or impracticable for a defendant to purchase natural gas at the "take-or-pay" contract price despite an extreme deviation between that price and the market value of the gas caused by governmental regulation and financial hardship, because "a more than twofold increase in the cost of performing [did] not alter the essential nature of performance."

The event that makes performance impossible or impracticable cannot be reasonably foreseeable when the parties made the contract. An event is deemed foreseeable if the parties allocated the risk of its occurrence in the contract.

Oklahoma courts have applied these principles to hold: the parties to a settlement agreement requiring the defendant to use the plaintiff as a back-up machine operator reasonably assumed there would be a continued need for operators and back-up operators; a basic assumption of the parties' shipping agreement was that if the railroad ceased to exist, the contract would be dissolved and the railroad's nonperformance would be excused; and the parties to a lease never contemplated their agreement to repair included rebuilding a leased hotel after a tornado destroyed it.

On the other hand, courts in Oklahoma have held: the parties to a swine purchasing agreement reasonably foresaw the market price could fall to one-third or one-sixth of the agreed floor price; a consultant and casino developer "had every reason to anticipate" that the developer's subsidiary could fail to obtain required financing, where the contract acknowledged the risk that pre-development opportunities may not lead to permanent opportunities; a gas-purchaser assumed the risk of an extreme disparity between the contract price and the market value of gas when it agreed to purchase gas at a fixed price subject to redetermination based on the highest price paid in a four-county area; and "world-wide glut of oil, a severe national economic recession, foreign commodity competition, abnormally warm weather during 19821983, price-induced consumer energy conservation and a sudden, wholly unexpected, unanticipated and unforeseeable change in the natural gas market because of the worldwide glut of oil were exactly the type of risks that business contracts made at fixed prices are intended to cover.ii

The coronavirus and related government action are clearly outside of companies' control and not something they could have reasonably foreseen. The absence of a force majeure clause may actually strengthen the argument that the risk of a pandemic was not allocated in a contract. As a result, we expect companies' ability to successfully assert these defenses will primarily turn on the extent to which performing would actually cause extreme and unreasonable difficulty, expense, injury, or loss. This is a fact-intensive inquiry and must be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Companies must use reasonable efforts to overcome any obstacles to performance and must continue to perform those portions of their obligations that are not impossible or impracticable.

Companies should also be aware of the related common law defense of frustration of purpose. Even if performance likely remains possible or practicable, companies may avoid or limit their contractual obligations if coronavirus or related government action has substantially frustrated the principal purpose of the contract. It is not enough for the contract to become less profitable or for the affected party to sustain a loss; the frustration must be so severe that it cannot fairly be regarded as within the risks assumed under the contract. For example, one court held the principal purpose of a car rental franchise agreement was not impaired by a hurricane because rental cars remained intact and the franchise conducted some business immediately following the hurricane.

Even in the absence of a force majeure clause or strong common law defense, companies can still take steps to protect themselves, such as reviewing their contract's termination clause or negotiating with the other party to amend or suspend performance.

As the coronavirus and governmental response continue to unfold, companies and their counter-parties should expect to face increased challenges to performing their contractual obligations. Companies should be proactive and begin the process now of carefully reviewing their contracts to determine their rights and obligations as to force majeure (and termination). Even in the absence of a force majeure clause, companies should be aware they may have a legal basis under Oklahoma law to avoid or limit contractual obligations that have become impossible or impracticable to perform. Companies that intend to rely on these defenses must take all reasonable steps to meet their contractual obligations and continue to perform those portions of their obligations that are not impossible or impracticable.

Dear Honorable Mayor Rahm Emanuel,

As a dedicated city planner for the City of Chicago, I am writing this letter to bring to your attention three pressing issues that require immediate action. As a responsible civic leader, I have devised practical solutions to address these challenges. I am confident that implementing these proposals will positively impact our community and contribute to the continued growth and prosperity of our beloved city.

Issue #1: Public Safety

One of the most critical concerns facing our city is public safety. The recent surge in violent crimes, particularly in some neighborhoods, has left residents feeling uneasy and vulnerable. To mitigate this problem, I suggest enhancing police presence in high-crime areas through the deployment of more officers on foot and bike patrols. This strategy would enable law enforcement officials to interact with communities and gather intelligence that could lead to the apprehension of criminal elements. Additionally, the implementation of more advanced technology such as gunshot detection systems and surveillance cameras would aid in quicker response times and facilitate the identification and arrest of offenders.

Issue #2: Affordable Housing

Another significant challenge facing our city is affordable housing. The increasing cost of living in Chicago has forced many residents to relocate or become homeless. To combat this issue, I recommend exploring alternative funding sources for affordable housing projects, including federal grants, private sector partnerships, and tax incentives. Furthermore, we should prioritize preserving existing affordable housing units by providing subsidies to landlords to keep rent prices low. Lastly, promoting mixed-income developments that incorporate both affordable and market-rate housing would create a diverse community and promote social integration.

Issue #3: Infrastructure Development

Infrastructure development is essential to support economic growth and improve the quality of life for residents. However, there are several deficiencies in our current infrastructure that need addressing. Firstly, we must invest in upgrading our transportation system, including improving public transit routes, expanding bike lanes, and constructing new pedestrian walkways. Secondly, we should explore innovative ways to manage stormwater runoff, such as green roofs, rain gardens, and permeable pavements, to reduce flooding during heavy rainfalls. Thirdly, we ought to prioritize maintaining existing infrastructure, such as roads, bridges, and buildings, through regular inspections and repairs to avoid costly replacements.

Albert Delin  (17 April 1712, Ath – 26 Nov 1771, Tournai; also known as Albertus Delin) was a harpsichord maker in the Low Countries.

Biography
Born in Ath in Southern Netherlands (now in Belgium), he soon moved to the nearby town of Tournai to practice his trade. Little is known of his training but a remarkable number of his instruments have survived. His building style is quite contrary to his more famous contemporaries, like his neighbours Dulckens in Antwerp, the Hass family in Hamburg or the Taskins of Paris, that at the time created complex machines with an extensive variety of registers and knee levers. Delin's surviving instruments are simple, reminiscent of the old Ruckers instruments of a century before and of good workmanship as witnessed by the number of surviving instruments.

Surviving instruments
Two surviving harpsichords (1750 and1768), both have a single manual and have only two 8' choirs and a buff stop, with all battens protruding through the instruments side, similar to original Ruckers instruments.
Kottick mentions four bentside spinets (1763, 1765, 1766, 1770), all with a single 8' choir.  A colorful fifth bentside spinet signed "A.D. 1738" and bearing a rose with the initials AD, has been attributed to him as well.
Three clavicytheria (1751, 1752, 1760), strung like his harpsichords with two 8' registers, and guidebattens protruding through the cheek. The clavicytheria have an elegant pivot mechanism of Delins' own design, needing no spring action and only gravity for the return. Chung describes Delins clavicytherium thus: "[he] succeeded in overcoming the difficulties of building an upright harpsichord better than any other builder. His three instruments, which are considered by many to be the finest of all surviving clavicytheria, have an amazingly fine touch that is achieved by a special action that upon the release of the keys allows the jacks to return without the need of springs or additional weights."
The last surviving instrument is even more old fashioned than the rest, a small, hexagonal, octave spinet (1750).

Decor of the instruments
Delin's original case decor seems to have been simple, but some of his instruments later received "makeovers". The 1738 spinet is elaborately painted with a forest scene on the inside of the lid, while the case is covered with a menagerie of monkeys playing musical instruments.

prompt: What are some interesting facts about twins?
response_a:
1. Identical twins (monozygotic) develop from a single fertilized egg that splits into two embryos, while fraternal twins (dizygotic) occur when two eggs are released and fertilized separately by different sperm.

2. According to statistics, approximately one in every 250 pregnancies results in the birth of twins. This number has increased over time due to advanced reproductive technologies such as in vitro fertilization (IVF).

3. Some identical twins can be right-handed, while their siblings are left-handed, which suggests that genetics plays a role in determining handedness, but environmental factors also contribute.

4. Studies have shown that twins raised apart often share similar personality traits, preferences, and even career choices, indicating a strong genetic component in personality development.

5. Twins can experience unique health challenges, such as twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), a condition where blood flow is unequal between identical fetuses sharing a placenta. In severe cases, surgery may be necessary to separate the blood vessels in the placenta.

6. Twinning can affect fertility; women carrying twins have higher risks of pregnancy complications, such as preterm labor or gestational diabetes.

7. Famous twins include celebrities like the Olsen twins, Mary-Kate and Ashley, as well as political figures such as former US President James Garfield, who had an identical brother who died before birth.

8. In rare instances, twins can have different fathers, known as heteropaterny or superfecundation, resulting from ovulation twice during a menstrual cycle.

9. Twins have been used in scientific research to study genetics, including studies on genes associated with specific diseases, such as Alzheimer's or breast cancer.

10. The world's oldest living twins, Catherine and Frank Rossiter, were born on April 15, 1912, in England, making them 108 years old as of 2020. They hold the Guinness World Record for the oldest living twins.
response_b:
1. Identical twins share the same DNA: This is because they develop from a single fertilized egg that splits into two embryos. As a result, they have identical genetic makeup.

2. Fraternal twins can be of different genders: Unlike identical twins, fraternal twins develop from two separate eggs that are fertilized by two sperm cells. This means that they can be of different genders.

3. Twins can be born minutes or years apart: In rare cases, twins can be born at very different times due to factors such as chorionic gestation (when twins share a placenta) or superfetation (when a woman becomes pregnant with twins at different times).

4. Twins may have distinct personalities: While genetics play a role in personality development, environment and experiences also shape who we become. As such, it's possible for twins to have unique personalities despite sharing the same genes.

5. Some twins have different blood types: Although identical twins share the same DNA, there are certain genetic mutations that can cause differences in blood type. This occurs more frequently in monozygotic (identical) twins than in dizygotic (fraternal) twins.

6. Twin studies help us understand genetics: By comparing the traits and characteristics of identical and fraternal twins, researchers can better understand the role of genetics in human development.

7. Twins often have a strong bond: Growing up together, twins often develop a close relationship that can last a lifetime. This connection has been attributed to shared experiences, similar interests, and the unique dynamics of being a twin.

8. Twinning rates are increasing: The rate of twin births has been on the rise in recent decades, although the exact reasons for this trend are not fully understood. It could be due to factors such as increased use of assisted reproductive technologies, older maternal age, and changes in lifestyle habits.

9. Twins can experience health challenges: Being a twin does not guarantee good health, as twins can still face health issues such as premature birth, low birth weight, and congenital anomalies. However, research suggests that twins may have lower rates of chronic diseases such as diabetes and heart disease compared to singletons.
